Rust is fast by default, but "fast by default" is not the same as "fast in your program". This module is about measuring first and changing second.

The rule

Never optimise without a measurement. Every section below assumes you have a profile or a benchmark in hand. Intuition about performance is wrong often enough that guessing is a waste of time.

Step 1: build for measurement

Then strip for the shipped binary (strip = "symbols" in a separate profile).

Step 2: profile

Linux: perf

--call-graph dwarf needs debug = true and gives readable stacks.

Flame graphs

Wide bars are where the time goes. Look for the widest leaf frame — that is actual work, not the call chain above it.

macOS: Instruments, samply

samply opens a Firefox Profiler UI with a timeline — better than flame graphs for async code, because it shows idle time separately.

Async profiling

Flame graphs of async code show the executor, not your tasks. For tokio, enable tokio-console:

You get per-task poll counts, busy time, wakeups, and — most importantly — tasks that are blocked for a long time.

Step 3: the usual wins, in order

1. Algorithm and data structure

Nothing else competes. A HashMap lookup instead of a linear scan inside a loop is a 1000× win; no compiler flag comes close.

2. Allocations

Every String/Vec/format! allocates. In a hot loop this dominates.

Consider SmallVec<[T; 8]> when most vectors stay small — it avoids the heap entirely for ≤ 8 items.

3. Cloning

cargo clippy flags some of these with redundant_clone; the rest you find in a profile.

4. I/O buffering

Same for reading: BufReader. For very large files, memmap2 avoids copying altogether.

5. Bounds checks

Iterators usually eliminate them:

When you genuinely need indexed access and have proven safety, get_unchecked in an unsafe block removes the check — but measure first; modern CPUs predict bounds checks almost perfectly and the win is often zero.

6. String building

7. Hashing

The default SipHash in HashMap is DoS-resistant and slow. For trusted, internal keys, ahash or rustc-hash is 2–3× faster:

Do not do this for a map keyed by untrusted input — you lose hash-flooding protection.

8. Vec growth patterns

9. Compile flags

target-cpu=native enables AVX2/AVX-512 and is worth 5–20% on numeric code — but the binary then may not run on older CPUs. In containers, build with an explicit target-cpu=x86-64-v3 instead.

10. Parallelism

After everything else, use rayon:

Only after the single-threaded version is tight. Parallelising a slow algorithm just makes it slow in parallel.

Reading perf stat

  • IPC < 1.0 — usually memory-bound or branch-heavy, not compute-bound. Look at data layout.
  • High branch-misses — unpredictable branches. Sorting input first, or branchless code, helps.
  • High cache-misses — the working set does not fit in cache. Restructure to arrays of structs → struct of arrays.

Struct of arrays vs array of structs

SoA vectorises: for x in &p.x { *x += 1.0 } is a clean SIMD loop. AoS forces gather/scatter. This is a 2–10× difference in numeric kernels.

Zero-cost abstractions: what is actually free

Free (compiled away):

  • iterators and closures (after inlining)
  • generics and monomorphisation
  • newtypes
  • Option<&T> (niche optimisation)
  • #[inline] on small functions

Not free:

  • dyn Trait dispatch (one indirect call, blocks inlining)
  • Box/Rc/Arc (allocation and counting)
  • format! (allocation)
  • RefCell (runtime borrow flag)
  • clone() (obvious, but easy to miss inside a chain)

Benchmarks that lie

Trap Fix
Debug build Always --release / criterion
Optimiser removes the work black_box(input) and black_box(result)
One run, cold cache criterion runs many iterations and reports statistics
Unrealistic input Benchmark with production-sized, production-shaped data
Benchmarking the setup Hoist setup out of the timed closure
Comparing micro-opts with no profile Measure end-to-end first

Exercises

  1. Generate a flame graph for a program with an obvious hot loop. Identify the widest leaf frame.
  2. Take count_words and measure both versions with criterion. Report the ratio and the allocation count (use a counting allocator).
  3. Convert an AoS Vec<Particle> to SoA and benchmark a physics step.
  4. Run perf stat on a hot loop and report IPC. Is it compute- or memory-bound?
  5. Replace HashMap with AHashMap in a benchmark and measure the difference.
  6. Add BufWriter to a file-writing loop and measure the speedup on 1M lines.
